request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Hospital Course:
The patient, an 85-year-old male, was admitted to the hospital with bilateral foot swelling, decreased urine output, and a poor urinary stream. He also complained of breathlessness, anorexia, weight loss, and had a past medical history significant for anemia. Physical examination revealed multiple, nontender, firm lymph nodes in the right upper jugular, middle jugular, right and left submandibular, and multiple right-sided axillary lymph nodes. His laboratory investigations revealed findings consistent with tumor lysis syndrome, including elevated uric acid, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia. Bone marrow examination showed hypercellular smears with reduced megakaryocytes and erythropoiesis. The bone marrow differential counts revealed immature cells with monocytic differentiation and large collections of mature lymphocytes.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
Despite being explained about the treatment options and prognosis, the patient refused to undergo any further investigations and therapy.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged home in fair condition. A follow-up plan was initiated with further medical management as an outpatient.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The picture is an elderly man with generalized lymphadenopathy and tumor lysis syndrome. The bone marrow shows immature cells with monocytic differentiation alongside large collections of mature lymphocytes. This suggests a hematologic malignancy, most likely chronic lymphocytic leukemia with a concurrent myeloid process such as chronic myelomonocytic leukemia or acute myeloid leukemia with monocytic differentiation. The withheld diagnosis may be something like "chronic lymphocytic leukemia with acute monocytic leukemia" or "CLL with CMML."

The two candidates are C92 (myeloid leukemia, including CMML as C93.1 under monocytic leukemia) and C91 (lymphoid leukemia, including CLL as C91.1). The immature monocytic cells would be coded to C93 (monocytic leukemia), and large collections of mature lymphocytes point to C91.1.

The tumor lysis syndrome (E88.3) is a complication of the malignancy, so the malignancy is the principal diagnosis. Of the options, the lymphadenopathy and mature lymphocytes make CLL plausible. However, the immature monocytic cells and the tumor lysis syndrome suggest an acute process, so the monocytic leukemia is likely the more active condition driving this admission. The reduced megakaryocytes and erythropoiesis with immature monocytic cells point to a marrow-replacing acute or chronic monocytic leukemia.

I'll go with C93, the monocytic leukemia category.

CODE: C93
